CHAPTER 0The Big Picture: What Is VLSI?

Before any formulas: what are we even building, and why do we start with tiny bits of crystal?

Your notes p.1 (header list)
Explain like I'm 10

Imagine building a huge city out of LEGO. If you glue each brick by hand, one at a time, a city with a billion bricks would take forever. An integrated circuit (IC) is like a machine that prints the whole LEGO city at once on a piece of sand the size of your fingernail. VLSI (Very Large Scale Integration) just means the city has a very huge number of tiny buildings (transistors).

A transistor is a tiny switch. Millions of switches, wired together, can add numbers, remember things and run games. To make good switches we need a special material that can be a wire or a wall whenever we choose: that material is a semiconductor. That is why the whole course starts with semiconductors.

Discrete vs Integrated

  • Discrete circuit: separate components (resistors, transistors, capacitors) soldered onto a board with wires. Big, slow, expensive to build in large numbers.
  • Integrated circuit (IC): all those components made together, on one small piece of silicon, in one manufacturing process. Small, fast, cheap, low power.

SSI, MSI, LSI, VLSI: counting the switches

LevelNameRoughly how many gates / transistorsExample
SSISmall-Scale Integrationfewer than 10 gatesa single logic-gate chip (7400 NAND)
MSIMedium-Scale10 to 100 gatescounters, multiplexers, decoders
LSILarge-Scale100 to about 10,000 gatesearly microprocessors, small memories
VLSIVery-Large-Scale10,000 to about 1,000,000 gates1980s-90s microprocessors
ULSIUltra-Large-Scaleabove a million (today: billions of transistors)modern phone / laptop chips
Beyond your notes

Exact boundaries differ by textbook (some count transistors, some count gates). If a question asks "define VLSI", say "more than about 104 to 106 transistors/gates on a single chip" and mention the trend: the number of transistors per chip roughly doubles every two years (Moore's law).

The road map of this course (your "Unit 1")

Your notes list Unit 1 as two halves. Everything below follows exactly this order:

Half A: Material physics

  1. Semiconductor materials, crystal structure
  2. Energy bands, E–k diagram, effective mass, holes
  3. Fermi–Dirac statistics, density of states
  4. Doping and carrier concentration
  5. Drift, diffusion, mobility, recombination

Half B: Devices

  1. p–n junction diode
  2. BJT (bipolar junction transistor)
  3. MOS capacitor
  4. MOSFET (the switch inside every VLSI chip)
  5. CMOS (nMOS + pMOS together)
The story in one breath

Crystals have energy "floors" (bands) → electrons and holes live on those floors → we control how many there are by adding impurities (doping) → they move by pushing (drift) and by spreading out (diffusion) → put a p-piece next to an n-piece and you get a one-way gate (diode) → stack three pieces and a small current controls a big one (BJT) → or use an electric field through an insulator to open and close a channel (MOSFET) → pair two kinds of MOSFET and you get a switch that uses almost no power when idle (CMOS), the building block of VLSI.

CHAPTER 1Semiconductors and Energy Bands

What makes a material a metal, an insulator or a semiconductor? The answer is a picture of energy shelves.

Your notes p.1 to p.3

1.1 What is a semiconductor?

Your notes say

A semiconductor is a material whose conductivity can be tuned by many orders of magnitude. Applications: (i) switch, (ii) amplifier, (iii) logic device, (iv) LED, solar cells, photodetectors, (v) the whole electronics industry.

Explain like I'm 10

Copper is like a wide-open highway: cars (electrons) run freely. Glass is like a highway with a giant wall across it: nothing gets through. A semiconductor is a highway with a small gate. If you give it a tiny push (heat, light, a little chemical "seasoning" called doping, or a voltage) the gate opens. Because we decide when it opens, we can make switches and amplifiers.

Typical conductivity numbers (in S/cm), so you can feel "many orders of magnitude":

Material typeConductivity σ (S/cm)Example
Metal104 to 106copper, aluminium
Semiconductor10-8 to 103 (tunable!)silicon: from about 4×10-6 pure to 103 heavily doped
Insulatorbelow 10-12glass, SiO2

1.2 Elemental vs compound semiconductors

Elemental

Made of one kind of atom, from group IV of the periodic table.

Examples: Si (silicon), Ge (germanium).

Compound

Made of two or more elements, e.g. group III + group V.

Examples: GaAs (gallium arsenide), GaN (gallium nitride).

Beyond your notes: crystal structure

Your Unit-1 list starts with "crystal structure". Silicon and germanium atoms sit in a diamond cubic lattice: every atom has 4 nearest neighbours and shares one electron with each (a covalent bond), so every atom "feels" it has 8 outer electrons. GaAs uses the very similar zinc-blende lattice (Ga and As alternate). A crystal means the atoms repeat in a perfectly regular pattern; this regularity is what creates energy bands.

1.3 Energy bands: valence band, conduction band, band gap

Explain like I'm 10

Think of a two-storey building for electrons. The ground floor is the valence band (VB): it is crowded, everybody is packed in and cannot move around. The top floor is the conduction band (CB): it is empty and roomy, so anyone who gets up there can run about and carry electricity. Between the floors there is empty space where nobody can stand: the energy band gap Eg. To climb from ground floor to top floor an electron needs at least Eg of energy (from heat or light).

MetalSemiconductorInsulator
Band gapnone (bands overlap)small (about 0.5 to 3.5 eV)very large (more than about 4 to 5 eV)
Free electrons at room temperaturehuge numberfew, but adjustablepractically none
Resistivity when temperature risesincreasesdecreases (more carriers)decreases slightly
Your notes say

Metals: the VB and CB touch/overlap. Insulators: Eg "very greater". Semiconductors: Eg "lesser". Eg = energy difference between the lowest level of the CB and the highest level of the VB.

1.4 Where do bands come from? (Formation of energy bands)

Your notes use carbon as the example (silicon behaves the same way, just one shell down).

Explain like I'm 10

One lonely atom has its own private "rooms" (energy levels): exact, single rooms. Now bring many atoms close together. Electrons from neighbouring atoms start to influence each other, and the rules of quantum physics say two electrons can't have exactly the same energy. So the single room of every atom is nudged a tiny bit up or down from its neighbours', and a huge crowd of almost-identical rooms forms a smooth-looking band, like a stairway so finely stepped that it looks like a ramp.

Step by step with carbon (Z = 6)

  1. Electron configuration: 1s2 2s2 2p2. Inner 1s stays tightly bound; the action is in the outer shell (2s and 2p).
  2. Number of states: an s-level has 2 states (spin up/down), a p-level has 6 states (three orbitals × 2 spins). Your notes list 1s: 2, 2s: 2, 2p: 6.
  3. Electrons available: 2s holds 2 electrons, 2p holds only 2 of its 6 states. So each atom has 4 outer electrons and 8 outer states (2 + 6).
  4. For N atoms: 8N states and 4N electrons. (Your notes: "6N states, 2N electrons" for p, "2N states, 2N electrons" for s.)
  5. As the atoms come closer, the 2s level and 2p level spread into bands, then merge and re-split into two bands of 4N states each. The lower one holds all 4N electrons: full = valence band. The upper one is empty = conduction band. The empty region between them is Eg.
Counting rule
N atoms → 8N outer states, 4N outer electrons → VB: 4N states (full), CB: 4N states (empty at 0 K)

1.5 Band-gap values you must remember

MaterialEg at 300 K (from your notes)Type
Ge0.7 eVelemental, indirect
Si1.1 eV (more precisely 1.12)elemental, indirect
GaAs1.34 eV (textbooks: 1.42)compound, direct
GaN3.4 eVcompound, direct

Order for exams: Ge (0.7) < Si (1.1) < GaAs (1.34) < GaN (3.4).

GaN's big gap is why it emits blue light and handles high voltages; Ge's tiny gap is why Ge devices leak a lot and turn on at lower voltage.

1.6 Thermal energy of an electron

Heat gives electrons random kicks. The typical kick size is kBT.

Thermal energy
Ethermal = kBT    with kB = 1.38×10-23 J/K (Boltzmann constant)
At T = 300 K: E = 300 × 1.38×10-231.6×10-19 ≈ 25.87 meV ≈ 26 meV ≈ 0.026 eV

The division by 1.6×10-19 converts joules to electron-volts (1 eV = 1.6×10-19 J).

Explain like I'm 10

Silicon's gap is 1.1 eV but a typical heat kick is only 0.026 eV, roughly 42 times too small. So heat alone almost never lifts an electron across the gap, and only a rare, lucky electron makes it. That is why pure silicon at room temperature is such a poor conductor, and why doping is needed.

Worked question. How many times bigger than kBT at 300 K is the silicon band gap? What if T = 600 K?

Eg/kBT = 1.1 / 0.02585 ≈ 42.6 at 300 K. At 600 K, kBT doubles to 0.0517 eV, so the ratio is 1.1/0.0517 ≈ 21.3. The exponent in ni ∝ e-Eg/2kBT halves, so ni grows enormously with temperature.

Exam traps for this chapter
  • Don't say "electrons are in the band gap". The gap is forbidden: no allowed states.
  • Metals have no gap because bands overlap, not because the gap is zero-sized in a semiconductor sense.
  • Always convert: 1 eV = 1.6×10-19 J. Forgetting this gives answers off by 1019.

CHAPTER 2The E–k Diagram, Effective Mass, Holes

A map that tells you how an electron behaves inside a crystal, and why an electron in silicon acts as if it had a different mass.

Your notes p.4 to p.7

2.1 What are k and the E–k diagram?

Explain like I'm 10

You can describe a song in two ways: as the wiggly sound in time, or as a list of which notes (frequencies) it contains. Both describe the same song. The switch between them is called a Fourier transform. Electrons are waves too. We can describe them by where they are (real space, in cm) or by how fast the wave wiggles in space (reciprocal space, in cm-1). That second number is k, the wave-vector. More wiggles per centimetre = bigger k = faster electron.

Real domainFourier transform →Reciprocal domain
time (s)F.T.frequency ω
real space (cm)F.T.reciprocal space (cm-1)
wavelength λ (cm)F.T.k = 2π/λ (cm-1), the wave-vector

Derivation from your notes: ħk is momentum

Momentum of the electron wave
ħk = ħ · 2πλ = h2π · 2πλ = hλ = p   ⇒  p = ħk
(ħ = h/2π is the reduced Planck constant; h/λ is the de Broglie momentum.)

Free-electron energy

Kinetic energy → parabola
K.E. = ½ m v² = p²2m  ⇒  E = ħ²k²2m

So for a lone electron E versus k is a parabola (left plot below). For an electron in a crystal, the periodic atoms cut the parabola into pieces and open gaps exactly at k = ±π/a, ±2π/a, … (a = lattice spacing). Those gaps are the band gaps (right plot).

Beyond your notes: why gaps appear at ±π/a

An electron wave whose wavelength is exactly twice the lattice spacing (λ = 2a, so k = π/a) gets reflected by each layer of atoms (Bragg reflection). Reflected and forward waves combine into two standing waves: one piles up charge on the atoms (lower energy) and one between the atoms (higher energy). The energy difference between them is the gap.

2.2 Effective mass m*

Near the bottom of a band the crystal E–k curve still looks like a parabola, but a different one. We keep the free-electron formula and just swap the mass:

Effective-mass parabola
E = ħ²k²2m*  where m* = effective mass of the electron

Getting m* from the curve (your derivation)

E = ħ²k²2m*  ⇒  dEdk = ħ²km*  ⇒  d²Edk² = ħ²m*
m* = ħ²d²E/dk²  ← inverse of the curvature of the E–k diagram
Explain like I'm 10

Pushing a shopping cart through a quiet hall is easy. Pushing the same cart through a crowded market is hard because people keep bumping it. The cart hasn't gotten heavier; the crowd is just interfering. An electron in a crystal is being pushed and pulled by all the atoms, so it responds to a force as if it had a new mass, the effective mass. Steep, sharply curved E–k = light and nimble electron. Flat, lazy E–k = heavy, sluggish electron.

Remember
high curvature ⇒ low m* ⇒ high mobility ⇒ high current density
low curvature (flat) ⇒ high m* ⇒ low mobility ⇒ low current density
Your notes' question: two semiconductors have the E–k curves below. Which has the higher current density?

Semiconductor 1's curve is sharper (higher curvature) than semiconductor 2's. So:

  1. Curvature ↑ ⇒ m* = ħ²/(d²E/dk²) ↓.
  2. Since μ = qτ/m*, a smaller m* gives a higher mobility.
  3. J = nqμE, so a higher μ gives a higher current density (same n, same E).

Answer: semiconductor 1 (the higher-curvature one).

Careful with the numbers

Your page also shows m* = 0.2m0 and m* = 0.06m0 (struck through). If a question gives numbers, compare them directly: the smaller m* always wins. With those two values the 0.06m0 material has the higher mobility, so it would have to be the one drawn with the higher curvature. Always match the curve to its mass before answering. (m0 = 9.11×10-31 kg is the free-electron mass.)

Extra: an E–k curve is E = 2×10-38 k² (E in J, k in m-1). Find m* in terms of m0.

Compare with E = ħ²k²/2m*: ħ²/2m* = 2×10-38. With ħ = 1.055×10-34 J·s, ħ² = 1.113×10-68. So m* = ħ²/(2 × 2×10-38) = 1.113×10-68 / 4×10-38 = 2.78×10-31 kg ≈ 0.31 m0.

2.3 Holes

Your notes say

A hole is the absence of an electron, modelled as a positively charged particle. It always moves in the valence band. mh* = effective mass of holes, me* = effective mass of electrons.

Explain like I'm 10

A parking lot is completely full except for one empty space. When a car moves into the empty space, a new empty space appears where it came from, so the empty space seems to travel backwards. Tracking the one empty space is much easier than tracking 100 cars. The moving empty space is the hole. It acts like a tiny positive charge that moves in the direction of the electric field, while electrons go the opposite way.

  • When an electron jumps from the VB to the CB it leaves a hole behind: an electron–hole pair (EHP) is created.
  • Electrons in the CB and holes in the VB both carry current.
  • In a hole picture the valence-band E–k curve is turned upside down (a hill), and the hole's effective mass is given the positive sign.
  • In Si, mh* > me* (holes are heavier), so holes are slower: μp < μn.

2.4 Ec, Ev and Eg on the E–k diagram

Ec = lowest point of the conduction band, Ev = highest point of the valence band, and Eg = Ec − Ev. Your notes draw the CB as an upward parabola sitting on top of the VB's downward parabola.

2.5 Direct and indirect band-gap semiconductors

Direct band-gapIndirect band-gap
ExamplesGaAs, GaNSi, Ge
Where are Ec and Ev?at the same k (both at k = 0)Ev at k = 0, Ec at k ≠ 0
To excite an electron VB → CBonly energy is neededenergy and momentum change; needs a phonon
Light emission (LED / laser)efficientpoor
Best forLEDs, lasers, solar cellsdigital chips (cheap, great oxide)
Explain like I'm 10

A phonon is a little shake of the crystal's atoms (heat vibration). A photon (light particle) carries plenty of energy but almost no momentum, like a ping-pong ball. Jumping straight up is easy. But in silicon the top floor's doorway is off to the side, so the electron needs a sideways shove as well. The atom vibration (phonon) provides that sideways shove, like a friend giving you a push at the same moment you jump. Needing two things to happen together makes silicon bad at making light.

Exam traps
  • Photons carry energy but negligible momentum; phonons carry momentum but little energy. That's why indirect transitions need both.
  • Silicon is indirect. Many students memorise "Si = direct" by mistake because it is the most common material.

CHAPTER 3Fermi–Dirac Statistics, Fermi Level, Density of States

How many electrons are actually sitting on the top floor? Two ingredients: how many seats exist, and how likely each seat is to be taken.

Your notes p.7 to p.9, p.11 to p.12

3.1 The Fermi–Dirac function f(E)

Probability that a state of energy E is occupied by an electron
f(E) = 11 + exp( (E − EF) / kBT )
1 − f(E) = probability the state is empty = probability of finding a hole
Explain like I'm 10

Imagine a huge cinema where the seats are the energy levels. The Fermi level EF is an invisible "50-50 line": a seat exactly at that height is taken half the time. Seats far below the line are nearly always taken; seats far above are nearly always empty. The temperature decides how blurry the line is. At absolute zero the line is razor sharp; when it is warm, a few kids from the lower rows jump to seats above the line.

Important: the Fermi level does not have to be a real seat. Your notes call it an "imaginary construct". It can sit in the forbidden gap where no seat exists.

The three cases your notes list at T = 0 K

Energyf(E) at T = 0 KMeaning
E < EF1every state below EF is completely filled
E = EF½ (50%)the borderline
E > EF0every state above EF is completely empty

Why? For T → 0, if E < EF the exponent (E−EF)/kBT → −∞, so e−∞ = 0 and f = 1/(1+0) = 1. If E > EF the exponent → +∞, e+∞ = ∞, so f = 0.

Your notes, Q1: At T = 300 K find the probability of occupation of a state at (a) E = EF + 0.1 eV, (b) E = EF − 0.1 eV.
  1. Thermal energy kBT ≈ 0.026 eV at 300 K.
  2. (a) Exponent = 0.1/0.026 = 3.846, e3.846 = 46.81. So f = 1/(1 + 46.81) = 0.0209 = 2.09 %.
  3. (b) Exponent = −3.846, e−3.846 = 0.0213. So f = 1/(1 + 0.0213) = 0.979 = 97.9 %.

Check: the two answers add to 100 %. This always happens: f(EF+Δ) + f(EF−Δ) = 1. The chance a state Δ above EF is filled equals the chance a state Δ below is empty. (With kBT = 0.02585 eV you get 2.05 % and 97.95 %; both are accepted.)

Your notes, Q2: Plot f(E) versus E at T = 0 K, 200 K, 300 K.

Draw the same axes for all three. At 0 K: a horizontal line at 1 dropping vertically to 0 at EF. At 200 K: a fairly steep S-curve through (EF, 0.5). At 300 K: a gentler S-curve, also through (EF, 0.5). The hotter the curve, the more its "shoulders" spread out, so the more states above EF are occupied and the more below are empty. See the figure above (the extra 600 K curve shows the trend continuing).

Extra: at what energy above EF is f = 1 % at 300 K?

0.01 = 1/(1+ex) ⇒ ex = 99 ⇒ x = ln 99 = 4.595. E − EF = 4.595 × 0.02585 = 0.119 eV. In general, f ≈ e−(E−EF)/kBT once E − EF ≫ kBT (the "Boltzmann tail").

3.2 Density of states g(E)

Your notes say

g(E) = number of energy states available per unit energy per unit volume. f(E) = probability that a state is occupied.

Explain like I'm 10

g(E) is how many seats exist at each height. f(E) is the chance each seat is occupied. To count how many kids are actually in the top-floor seats, multiply "seats at each height" by "chance each is taken" and add up all heights. That is what the integral does.

Electron concentration in the conduction band
n = ∫Ec∞ g(E) f(E) dE    (similarly p = ∫−∞Ev g(E)[1 − f(E)] dE)
Beyond your notes: the results of that integral

Near the band edges g(E) ∝ √(E − Ec) (3-D crystal). Using the Boltzmann tail of f, the integral gives:

n = Nc exp[ −(Ec − EF)/kBT ]    p = Nv exp[ −(EF − Ev)/kBT ]
n = ni exp[ (EF − Ei)/kBT ]    p = ni exp[ (Ei − EF)/kBT ]

Nc, Nv are the "effective densities of states" (about 2.8×1019 and 1.04×1019 cm-3 for Si at 300 K); Ei is the intrinsic (mid-gap) Fermi level. The message: the closer EF is to Ec, the more electrons; the closer to Ev, the more holes. Multiplying the two gives n·p = NcNve−Eg/kT = ni², the mass-action law of Chapter 5.

3.3 Where does EF sit? Intrinsic, n-type, p-type

TypeCarriersEF position
Intrinsic (pure)n = pnear the middle of the gap
n-typen > pcloser to Ec (upper half)
p-typep > ncloser to Ev (lower half)
Your notes say

As you increase the doping, EF shifts towards the conduction band for n-type and towards the valence band for p-type.

Explain like I'm 10

EF is like the water level in a tank next to two shelves. Add donors (extra electrons) and the level rises toward the top shelf (CB). Add acceptors (extra holes) and the level sinks toward the bottom shelf (VB). The water level tells you at a glance which carrier is the majority.

3.4 Reading band diagrams (very common exam question)

  1. Flat EF everywhere ⇒ the system is at equilibrium ⇒ no net current.
  2. Sloped EF ⇒ current is flowing through the device (not equilibrium).
  3. Sloped (tilted) Ec and Ev ⇒ an electric field exists. The steeper the tilt, the stronger the field.
  4. Electric field: E = (1/q) dEc/dx (derived in Chapter 7). Electrons roll downhill in energy on the diagram; holes float uphill.

CHAPTER 4Doping: Seasoning the Crystal

Pure silicon is a poor conductor. Add a pinch of the right impurity and the conductivity jumps by a factor of a million.

Your notes p.9

4.1 Intrinsic (pure) vs extrinsic (doped)

  • Intrinsic semiconductor: perfectly pure. Every free electron in the CB came from a broken bond and left a hole behind, so n = p = ni. For Si at 300 K, ni ≈ 1.5×1010 cm-3 (some textbooks and your notes' questions use 1010). Silicon has 5×1022 atoms/cm3, so only 1 atom in 3 trillion has given a free electron.
  • Extrinsic semiconductor: impurity atoms deliberately added ("doping").

4.2 n-type doping: pentavalent atoms (donors)

Explain like I'm 10

Silicon atoms hold hands with four neighbours, using four electrons each. Now replace one silicon by phosphorus, which arrives with five hand-holders. Four form the bonds; the fifth is a spare with nobody to hold hands with, so it wanders off easily and can carry electricity. The phosphorus is now missing one electron, so it becomes a stuck-in-place positive ion (P+). It can't move, because it's locked in the crystal.

  • Dopants: phosphorus (P), arsenic (As), antimony (Sb). They are called donors because they donate an electron.
  • Donor concentration: ND (atoms per cm3). Each ionised donor becomes a fixed positive charge ND+.
  • Energy picture: the spare electron sits at a donor level Ed just below Ec (about 45 meV for P in Si). At room temperature (kBT = 26 meV) nearly all of them get kicked into the CB.
  • Result: n ≫ p. Electrons are the majority carriers, holes the minority carriers. EF moves up toward Ec.

4.3 p-type doping: trivalent atoms (acceptors)

Explain like I'm 10

Replace one silicon by boron, which brings only three hand-holders. One bond is left with an empty hand, a hole. A neighbouring electron happily jumps in to fill it, which leaves an empty hand behind at the neighbour, and so the hole travels around. The boron has accepted an extra electron, so it becomes a fixed negative ion (B−).

  • Dopants: boron (B), aluminium (Al), gallium (Ga), indium (In). Called acceptors.
  • Concentration NA; ionised acceptors are fixed negative charges NA−.
  • Energy picture: the acceptor level Ea lies just above Ev. A VB electron easily hops onto it, leaving a hole in the VB.
  • Result: p ≫ n. Holes are the majority carriers. EF moves down toward Ev.
n-typep-type
Dopant valence5 (pentavalent)3 (trivalent)
Dopant namedonor (P, As, Sb)acceptor (B, Al, Ga)
Concentration symbolNDNA
Fixed ion left behindpositive ND+negative NA−
Extra level in the gapEd, just below EcEa, just above Ev
Majority / minorityelectrons / holesholes / electrons
EF moves towardconduction bandvalence band
Exam traps
  • n-type and p-type crystals are electrically neutral overall. "n" refers to the majority carrier being negative, not the crystal being charged.
  • The ion is immobile; only the electron or hole moves. This is what builds the depletion region later.
  • Doping adds carriers of one sign but the minority carrier count goes down (mass-action law, next chapter).
Beyond your notes: compensation

If both donors and acceptors are present, they cancel. The net doping is |ND − NA|, and the crystal is n-type if ND > NA, p-type otherwise. This is used in real fabrication (e.g. making an n-well inside a p-substrate).

CHAPTER 5Carrier Concentration: How Many Electrons and Holes?

Two simple laws, mass-action and charge neutrality, give you n and p for any doping.

Your notes p.10 to p.11

5.1 Mass-action law

Your notes say

At equilibrium, the product of electron and hole concentrations in a semiconductor is constant at a given temperature and independent of doping.

Mass-action law
n · p = ni²   (intrinsic: n = p = ni)
Explain like I'm 10

Imagine a see-saw with electrons on one side and holes on the other, and a rule that the two counts multiplied together always give the same number. If you pour 1,000 times more electrons in (n-type doping), holes must shrink by 1,000 times. More of one means proportionally less of the other. The reason: extra electrons bump into holes and annihilate them (recombination) until balance is restored.

Only two things change ni: the material (bigger Eg ⇒ smaller ni) and the temperature (hotter ⇒ much larger ni):

ni ∝ T3/2 exp( − Eg / 2kBT )

You will need this exact dependence for your assignment question (Si vs Ge diodes, Chapter 7).

5.2 Charge neutrality

A doped crystal is not charged overall. The positive charges must exactly balance the negative charges:

Charge neutrality
positive: holes p + ionised donors ND+    negative: electrons n + ionised acceptors NA−
p + ND = n + NA (assuming full ionisation)

5.3 The general solution (your derivation)

  1. Rewrite neutrality: n + (NA − ND) − p = 0.
  2. Multiply by n: n² + n(NA − ND) − np = 0.
  3. Use np = ni²: n² + (NA − ND) n − ni² = 0, a quadratic in n.
  4. Quadratic formula (take the + root because n must be positive):
n = −(NA − ND) + √( (NA − ND)² + 4ni² )2    then p = ni² / n

Equivalent and easier to remember: with net donor density (ND − NA),

n = (ND − NA) + √( (ND − NA)² + 4ni² )2

5.4 The two shortcuts you actually use

Case I: strongly n-type (ND ≫ NA)

n ≈ ND
p = ni² / ND

Case II: strongly p-type (NA ≫ ND)

p ≈ NA
n = ni² / NA

When are they valid? When the net doping is more than about 10× ni. Doping of 1015 to 1018 cm-3 in Si at room temperature (ni ≈ 1010) is far beyond that, so the shortcuts are always fine there. Use the full quadratic only when the net doping is comparable to ni (very light doping or very high temperature).

Worked: silicon at 300 K, ni = 1.5×1010 cm-3, doped with ND = 1016 cm-3 and nothing else. Find n, p and EF − Ei.
  1. ND ≫ ni, so n ≈ 1016 cm-3.
  2. p = ni²/n = (2.25×1020)/1016 = 2.25×104 cm-3. One hole for every 4.4×1011 electrons.
  3. EF − Ei = kBT ln(n/ni) = 0.02585 × ln(6.67×105) = 0.02585 × 13.41 = 0.347 eV above the mid-gap, so EF is close to Ec, as expected for n-type.
Worked: compensated sample, ND = 5×1016, NA = 2×1016 cm-3, ni = 1.5×1010. Find n and p.

Net = ND − NA = 3×1016 ≫ ni. So the sample is n-type with n ≈ 3×1016 and p = 2.25×1020/3×1016 = 7.5×103 cm-3.

Worked (when the shortcut fails): ni = 1010, net doping ND − NA = 1010 cm-3. Find n and p.

Doping is equal to ni, so use the full formula: n = [1010 + √(1020 + 4×1020)]/2 = [1010 + 2.236×1010]/2 = 1.618×1010 cm-3. Then p = 1020/1.618×1010 = 6.18×109 cm-3. Notice the shortcut (n = 1010) would be 38 % wrong here.

Extra: p-type Si with NA = 1017, ni = 1010. If the temperature rises until ni = 1017, what happens?

At that temperature ni equals the doping: the thermally generated carriers match the dopant-provided ones. The material stops behaving like p-type and starts behaving like intrinsic (n ≈ p). Full formula: p = [1017 + √(1034 + 4×1034)]/2 = 1.618×1017 and n = 6.18×1016. This is why silicon devices fail at very high temperature. A wide-gap material (GaN, SiC) reaches this point much later.

Exam traps
  • The mass-action product n·p = ni² only holds at equilibrium. Under light or injection, np > ni² (Chapter 6).
  • In the quadratic, take the + root. The − root gives negative n.
  • Units: concentrations are per cm3 in every formula in your notes, and mobilities are cm²/V·s. Mixing m3 and cm3 gives errors of 106.

CHAPTER 6Charge Transport: Drift, Mobility, Diffusion, Recombination

Carriers move for exactly two reasons: they get pushed by a field (drift) or they spread out from crowded to empty regions (diffusion).

Your notes p.12 to p.19

6.1 With no external push: random thermal motion

Your notes say (Case 1: no external excitation)

In an n-type bar with no field, electrons move at their thermal velocity in every direction and collide with (i) lattice atoms (which exchange energy as phonons) and (ii) impurity ions (ND+ or NA−), through Coulomb attraction. Result: net current = 0.

Explain like I'm 10

Picture a room full of bouncing balls, each going in a random direction very fast (about 107 cm/s for electrons in silicon at room temperature). For every ball going left another goes right, so nothing flows anywhere on average. It's busy but going nowhere.

6.2 Drift: applying an electric field

Your notes say (Case II: external electric field)

A net current appears: the drift current. The average speed of the net motion is the drift velocity Vd. Velocity = acceleration × time, with acceleration = F/m = qE/m*, and the time is the mean time between collisions τ (τ1, τ2, τ3… averaged).

Explain like I'm 10

Now tilt the room slightly so all the balls feel a gentle downhill push. They still bounce around randomly, but every time they start to speed up downhill they hit something and lose that extra speed. On average they creep slowly downhill. That slow creep is the drift velocity, tiny compared with the wild random speed, but it's the whole reason a current flows.

Drift velocity and mobility
Vd = acceleration × τ = qEm* · τ  ⇒  Vd = ( qτm* ) E = μ E
μ = qτm* (mobility, units cm²/V·s)   ← the slope of the Vd versus E line
  • Long τ (few collisions) ⇒ high mobility.
  • Small m* (light carrier) ⇒ high mobility.
  • Your notes' comparison: mh* > me* ⇒ Vd,hole < Vd,electron ⇒ μn > μp. In silicon at 300 K: μn ≈ 1350 and μp ≈ 450 cm²/V·s (the values your worked questions use). This is why nMOS is faster than pMOS, and why pMOS transistors are drawn ~2–3× wider in CMOS layouts.

6.3 How temperature changes mobility

Two scattering mechanisms fight for control. Each one has its own mobility, and they combine like resistors in parallel (the faster-acting scatterer dominates):

Matthiessen's rule
1μtotal = 1μphonon + 1μII
MechanismWhat happens when T risesWhy (your notes)
Phonon (lattice) scatteringμphonon decreasesTemp ↑ ⇒ atoms vibrate more ⇒ more collisions
Ionised-impurity scattering (μII)μII increasesTemp ↓ ⇒ electron's thermal energy ↓ ⇒ slow electrons are deflected more strongly by the charged ions. So μII ↓ when T ↓
Explain like I'm 10

Run past a stranger who is standing still with a big magnet. If you run fast you barely get pulled off course; if you jog slowly the magnet drags you around. That's impurity scattering: fast (hot) electrons zip past. But if it's too hot, the floor itself is shaking violently (phonons) and you keep tripping. Best running conditions are in the middle, so mobility has a peak.

Reading the curve: at low temperature the impurity scattering dominates (μ rises with T); at high temperature phonons dominate (μ falls with T). Because the smaller mobility wins in the reciprocal sum, μtotal follows whichever is worse, giving the hill.

6.4 Drift current density and conductivity

Drift current density (units A/cm²)
Jdrift = n q μn E + p q μp E = ( n q μn + p q μp ) E = σ E
σ = q ( n μn + p μp ) (conductivity, S/cm)    ρ = 1/σ (resistivity, Ω·cm)

n and p are in cm-3, so J = (cm-3)(C)(cm²/V·s)(V/cm) = A/cm². For an n-type bar the p-term is negligible, and vice versa.

Explain like I'm 10

Current = how many runners × how much each carries × how fast each runs. n and p are "how many runners", q is "how much each carries", μE is "how fast".

6.5 Velocity saturation

Your notes say

Low-E regime: Vd = μE (slope μ). High-E regime: Vd flattens at the saturation velocity Vmax. Reason: E ↑ ⇒ acceleration ↑ ⇒ K.E. ↑, but scattering also ↑ ⇒ K.E. ↓ (energy is dumped into the lattice).

Silicon's saturation velocity is about 107 cm/s for electrons. Beyond the point where μE reaches vsat, raising the field does not raise the speed any more, so the current in a short-channel MOSFET stops growing with voltage. This is important for modern (nanometre) transistors.

6.6 Diffusion

Explain like I'm 10

Spray perfume in a corner of a room. Very soon you smell it everywhere. No wind pushed it; the molecules simply jiggle randomly, and since there are far more of them in the corner, more of them wander out than wander in. Net result: a flow from crowded to empty. Charge carriers do the same, and because they carry charge, that flow is a diffusion current.

Your notes say

Inject charge carriers into one end of a bar. Diffusion current is due to a concentration gradient of charge carriers. For holes p(x) falling with x (dp/dx negative) the holes diffuse toward +x and hole current flows in +x. For electrons n(x) falling with x (dn/dx negative), electrons diffuse toward +x but the electron current flows toward −x (negative charge).

Diffusion current densities
Jn = + q Dn dn(x)dx     Jp = − q Dp dp(x)dx
Dn, Dp = diffusion coefficients (diffusivities), cm²/s

Sign logic: the particle flux always points down the gradient (−D dn/dx). Multiply by charge: electrons (−q) give +qDn dn/dx; holes (+q) give −qDp dp/dx. So both cases are the same flow of carriers but the electron current points opposite to the electron motion.

Beyond your notes: total current
Jn,total = q μn n E + q Dn dn/dx     Jp,total = q μp p E − q Dp dp/dx

In a real device both mechanisms act at once. In a p–n diode at equilibrium they cancel exactly.

6.7 Einstein's relation: drift and diffusion are cousins

Both are caused by the same thing: random thermal motion and collisions. So diffusivity and mobility must be linked:

Einstein relation
Dnμn = Dpμp = kBTq = VT ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K
Dn = μn VT    Dp = μp VT

VT = kBT/q is the thermal voltage. It shows up everywhere from here on (diode equation, built-in voltage, BJT). Memorise 25.9 mV (≈ 26 mV) at 300 K. Example: μn = 1350 ⇒ Dn = 1350 × 0.0259 = 35 cm²/s; μp = 450 ⇒ Dp = 11.7 cm²/s.

6.8 Generation and recombination

Explain like I'm 10

Generation is like a popcorn machine making new kernels: light or heat creates electron–hole pairs. Recombination is the opposite: an electron falls into a hole and both disappear (annihilate) releasing energy as heat or light. At equilibrium the two rates are equal, so the numbers stay steady.

In silicon most recombination doesn't happen band-to-band (that needs a phonon and is unlikely). Defects and impurities create trap states in the middle of the gap. An electron first drops into the trap (e⁻ capture), then the trap catches a hole (or emits the electron back: e⁻ emission). This is SRH recombination.

SRH net recombination rate
U = 1τ · pn − ni²p + n + 2ni    τ = lifetime of the charge carriers
  • Equilibrium (no excitation): pn = ni² ⇒ U = 0.
  • Non-equilibrium (extra carriers injected): p = p0 + Δp, n = n0 + Δn, where p0, n0 are the equilibrium values and Δp, Δn are generated by the external excitation (light, injection).
  • For low-level injection the rate simplifies to: n-type: U = Δp/τ (minority holes), p-type: U = Δn/τ (minority electrons).
  • Your note: the minority-carrier lifetime should be high in devices like solar cells, BJTs and diodes' base regions, so that injected carriers survive long enough to be collected.
Beyond your notes: diffusion length
Ln = √(Dn τn)    Lp = √(Dp τp)

It is the average distance an injected minority carrier travels before recombining. The diode chapter uses Ln, Lp heavily. Example: τ = 1 μs and Dp = 11.7 cm²/s ⇒ Lp = √(1.17×10-5) = 3.4×10-3 cm = 34 μm.

6.9 Your worked questions from class (all four, re-solved)

Q A. Electron concentration varies as n(x) = n0 + A x with A = −5×1015 cm-4. At 300 K, μn = 1200 cm²/V·s. Find the diffusion current density.
  1. Gradient: dn/dx = A = −5×1015 cm-4 (constant, so J is uniform).
  2. Einstein: Dn = μnVT = 1200 × 0.0259 = 31.08 cm²/s.
  3. Jn = q Dn dn/dx = 1.6×10-19 × 31.08 × (−5×1015) = −2.486×10-2 A/cm².

Jn ≈ −248.6×10-4 A/cm² ≈ −24.9 mA/cm² (your notes write it as −248.64×10-4). The negative sign means the current flows toward −x. Since the concentration falls with x, electrons diffuse toward +x, and their current (negative charge) is opposite: toward −x. ✔

Q B. p-type Si at 300 K: p = 5×1015 cm-3, ni = 1010 cm-3, μp = 450, μn = 1350 cm²/V·s. Find the conductivity.
  1. Minority electrons: n = ni²/p = 1020/5×1015 = 2×104 cm-3 (your notes: 0.2×105).
  2. σ = q(nμn + pμp) = 1.6×10-19 (2×104×1350 + 5×1015×450).
  3. First term = 2.7×107, second = 2.25×1018. Sum ≈ 2.25×1018.
  4. σ = 1.6×10-19 × 2.25×1018 = 0.36 S/cm (resistivity 2.78 Ω·cm).

The minority-electron term is 1011 times smaller, so it is safely ignored. Doping controls conductivity.

Q C. A uniform n-type Si bar, length 2 μm, has 1 V across it. ND = 1016 cm-3, μn = 1350 cm²/V·s. Find (a) drift velocity, (b) transit time, (c) drift current density, (d) resistance and drift current if the cross-section is 0.25 μm².

Convert first: L = 2 μm = 2×10-4 cm; area = 0.25 μm² = 0.25×10-8 = 2.5×10-9 cm².

  1. Field: E = V/L = 1/(2×10-4) = 5000 V/cm.
  2. (a) Vd = μE = 1350 × 5000 = 6.75×106 cm/s (your notes: 675×104 cm/s).
  3. (b) t = L/Vd = 2×10-4/6.75×106 = 2.96×10-11 s ≈ 30 ps.
  4. (c) J = ND q μn E = 1016 × 1.6×10-19 × 1350 × 5000 = 1.08×104 A/cm². (The intermediate 2.16 in your notes is σ = 2.16 S/cm.)
  5. (d) I = J × A = 1.08×104 × 2.5×10-9 = 2.7×10-5 A = 27 μA. R = V/I = 1/27 μA = ≈ 37 kΩ. Check with R = L/(σA) = 2×10-4/(2.16 × 2.5×10-9) = 37 kΩ ✔.
Trap

The tiny transit time (30 ps) is why a 2 μm silicon resistor can respond in the GHz range. Also note E = 5000 V/cm is already near the high-field region where velocity starts saturating, so the linear μE value is an idealisation.

Extra: intrinsic silicon at 300 K (ni = 1.5×1010). Find σ and ρ. Compare with the doped bar above.

σi = q ni(μn + μp) = 1.6×10-19 × 1.5×1010 × 1800 = 4.3×10-6 S/cm ⇒ ρ ≈ 2.3×105 Ω·cm. The n-type sample (ND = 1016) has σ = 2.16 S/cm: about 500,000 times better from one dopant atom in every five million silicon atoms. That is the meaning of "tunable by many orders of magnitude".

CHAPTER 7The p–n Junction Diode

Glue a p-type piece to an n-type piece and something magical appears: a one-way street for current.

Your notes p.19 to p.30

7.1 Physical structure

A p–n diode is one crystal, p-doped on one side and n-doped on the other, with a metal contact on each end. The p-side terminal is the anode and the n-side terminal is the cathode. The boundary is the metallurgical junction. The circuit symbol arrow points from anode to cathode, the direction conventional current is allowed to flow.

Explain like I'm 10

Two neighbouring playgrounds. Playground P has lots of empty swings (holes). Playground N has lots of kids (electrons). A one-way turnstile in the fence lets kids pass in only one direction. That fence-with-turnstile is the diode.

7.2 Open circuit: what happens the instant p meets n

  1. Concentration difference. The p-side is full of holes (p ≫ n) and the n-side full of electrons (n ≫ p). Your notes: "p>n" on the left and "n>p" on the right.
  2. Diffusion current ID. Holes diffuse from p to n; electrons diffuse from n to p. Both carriers moving this way make a conventional current from p to n. Your notes: "Diffusion current: p → n".
  3. A depletion region forms. When a hole leaves the p-side it leaves behind a fixed negative acceptor ion; when an electron leaves the n-side it leaves a fixed positive donor ion. Near the junction these uncovered charges pile up: Q− on the p-side, Q+ on the n-side. The region has almost no free carriers, hence depletion region (also called space-charge region).
  4. Built-in electric field. The + and − sheets create a field that points from the n-side to the p-side. This field is a hill (barrier) that opposes further diffusion. The voltage across it is the barrier potential (built-in voltage) V0.
  5. Drift current Idrift. The same field sweeps minority carriers across: electrons from the p-side to the n-side, holes from the n-side to the p-side. Drift current flows from n to p (conventional). Your notes: "Drift current is due to the movement of minority charge carriers"; it is also called the saturation current Is. Majority carriers: p on the p-side, n on the n-side. Minority: n on the p-side, p on the n-side.
  6. Equilibrium (open circuit). Diffusion grows until the barrier is high enough that the two currents are equal and opposite:
Equilibrium
Idiffusion = Idrift = Is ⇒ net current = 0
Explain like I'm 10

Kids from the N playground run into the P playground. But every kid who leaves makes the N side more "positive" (missing kids' friends) and every swing that gets filled makes the P side "negative". Soon there's an invisible wall of charge at the fence that pushes new kids back. When the pushback exactly equals the urge to run over, the traffic stops. That wall is the depletion region; its strength is V0.

7.3 The built-in voltage V0

Junction built-in voltage
V0 = VT ln( NA NDni² )
VT = kBT/q (thermal voltage), NA, ND = doping, ni = intrinsic concentration
Beyond your notes: one-line derivation

At equilibrium the electron concentration on the n-side (nn0 ≈ ND) and on the p-side (np0 = ni²/NA) differ by the Boltzmann factor of the barrier: nn0/np0 = eV0/VT. Therefore V0 = VT ln(NDNA/ni²).

  • Typical Si diodes: V0 ≈ 0.6 to 0.8 V; Ge: about 0.3 V. Heavier doping ⇒ larger V0 (only logarithmically).
  • You cannot measure V0 with a voltmeter across the open diode: the metal contacts create equal and opposite contact potentials.

7.4 Width of the depletion region and stored charge

Let the depletion region extend xp into the p-side and xn into the n-side, so the total width is W = xn + xp (your notes use ω).

Step 1: the two charge sheets are equal (charge neutrality of the whole diode)

|Q+| = q (A xn) ND    |Q−| = q (A xp) NA    (A = cross-section area)
|Q+| = |Q−| ⇒ xnxp = NAND
Explain like I'm 10

A see-saw again: the two sides must carry equal "weights". If one side has bricks packed 100× more densely, it only needs a layer 1/100 as thick. So the depletion region sinks deeper into the lightly doped side. If NA ≫ ND (a p⁺–n junction), then xn ≫ xp, and W ≈ xn.

Step 2: the width (given in your notes)

Depletion width (zero bias)
W = xn + xp = √( 2εsq ( 1NA + 1ND ) V0 )
εs = permittivity of the semiconductor; for Si: 1.04×10-12 F/cm (= 11.7 ε0)

Step 3: splitting W into xn and xp (your derivation)

  1. From xn/xp = NA/ND, add 1 to both sides: (xp + xn)/xp = (ND + NA)/ND.
  2. Since xp + xn = W:
xp = W · NDNA + ND     xn = W · NANA + ND

Notice the "crossover": xp carries ND (the other side's doping) in the numerator. A great way to remember it: the region on the lightly doped side is the wider one.

Step 4: charge stored on either side

Junction charge QJ = |Q+| = |Q−|
QJ = A q ( NA NDNA + ND ) W
QJ = A √( 2 εs q ( NA NDNA + ND ) V0 )
Worked (typical exam problem): a Si p–n junction has NA = 1018, ND = 1016 cm-3, ni = 1.5×1010, A = 10-4 cm², T = 300 K. Find V0, W, xn, xp, QJ. Then find W when 5 V reverse bias is applied.
  1. V0 = 0.0259 × ln(1018×1016 / 2.25×1020) = 0.0259 × ln(4.44×1013) = 0.0259 × 31.43 = 0.814 V.
  2. W = √[ (2×1.04×10-12 / 1.6×10-19) × (10-18 + 10-16) × 0.814 ] = √[1.3×107 × 1.01×10-16 × 0.814] = 3.27×10-5 cm = 0.327 μm.
  3. xn = W NA/(NA+ND) = 0.327 × 0.9901 = 0.323 μm, xp = 0.327 × 0.0099 = 0.0032 μm. Almost the whole region is on the lightly doped n-side, as predicted.
  4. QJ = A q [NAND/(NA+ND)] W = 10-4 × 1.6×10-19 × 9.9×1015 × 3.27×10-5 ≈ 5.2×10-12 C (5.2 pC).
  5. Reverse bias VR = 5 V: replace V0 by V0 + VR = 5.814 V. W scales with √(barrier): W = 0.327 × √(5.814/0.814) = 0.327 × 2.673 = 0.873 μm.

7.5 Energy-band diagram of the p–n junction

  1. Far from the junction, the p-side has EF near Ev, the n-side has EF near Ec.
  2. At equilibrium EF must be one flat line across the device (your note: "EF const ⇒ no current in the device").
  3. To keep EF flat, the p-side bands sit higher than the n-side bands. The bands bend through the depletion region. The bending is qV0 (your note: "slope in Ec and Ev ⇒ an electric field exists").
  4. Electrons on the n-side see a hill of height qV0 if they try to go to the p-side, and likewise holes.

Field from the band bending (your derivation)

Field: 𝓔 = − dV/dx  (1)    Electron energy: Ec = −qV ⇒ V = −Ec/q  (2)
Substitute (2) in (1): 𝓔 = 1q · dEcdx

The steeper Ec(x), the stronger the field. Zero slope ⇒ zero field (as in the neutral regions).

7.6 Applying a bias

Forward biasReverse bias
Connection+ to p (anode), − to n (cathode)+ to n, − to p
BarrierV0 − VF (smaller)V0 + VR (larger)
Depletion widthnarrower (ω ↓)wider (ω ↑)
CurrentsIdiffusion > IdriftIdrift > Idiffusion
Net currentlarge, grows exponentiallytiny: −Is, saturates
Explain like I'm 10

Forward: you lower the wall at the fence, so lots of kids pour across, and the current explodes as the wall gets lower. Reverse: you raise the wall even higher. Now nobody can cross except a rare few kids who are pushed across by the wall itself (the minority carriers), which gives a tiny, constant leakage current.

With reverse bias VR (in your notes)
W = √( 2εsq ( 1NA + 1ND ) (V0 + VR) )
QJ = A √( 2 εs q NA NDNA + ND (V0 + VR) )
(For forward bias replace V0 + VR by V0 − VF.)
Beyond your notes: junction capacitance

Because QJ changes with VR, a reverse-biased diode acts as a voltage-controlled capacitor: Cj = dQJ/dVR = εs A / W = Cj0 / √(1 + VR/V0). Wider W ⇒ smaller C. Used in varactor (tuning) diodes.

7.7 The current–voltage relation (deriving the diode equation)

Your notes derive this in five moves. Follow the story:

  1. Lower the barrier. Forward bias V reduces the barrier to V0 − V.
  2. Majority carriers diffuse over (electrons n → p side, holes p → n side).
  3. They become minority carriers on the other side: "injection of minority carriers". Let np0 = equilibrium electron concentration on the p-side (np0 = ni²/NA) and pn0 = ni²/ND on the n-side.
  4. Concentration right at the edge of the depletion region is boosted by the Boltzmann factor:
Edge-of-depletion-region concentrations (steady state)
pn(xn) = pn0 eV/VT     np(−xp) = np0 eV/VT
Excess (injected) holes at x = xn: pn0 eV/VT − pn0 = pn0(eV/VT − 1)
Excess electrons at x = −xp: np0(eV/VT − 1)
Explain like I'm 10

Each 60 mV (about 2.3 VT) of forward voltage multiplies the number of kids sneaking over by 10. So a small voltage change makes a huge change in the flow. That is why the forward curve is so steep.

  1. The injected carriers recombine as they wander deeper, so the excess decays exponentially with the diffusion length L:
pn(x) = pn0 + pn0(eV/VT − 1) e−(x − xn)/Lp
np(x) = np0 + np0(eV/VT − 1) e−x′/Ln (x′ = distance measured away from the junction edge at −xp; your notes write it as (x − xp))
Lp, Ln = diffusion lengths of holes and electrons
  1. Current from the gradient. Differentiate: dp/dx = −(1/Lp) × (excess) at the edge, so Jp = −q Dp dp/dx gives:
Jp(xn) = q DpLp pn0 (eV/VT − 1)     Jn(−xp) = q DnLn np0 (eV/VT − 1)
  1. Total current = hole part + electron part, both evaluated at the depletion edges (total current is the same everywhere in steady state; away from the junction it is carried by drift in the quasi-neutral regions, Jp = pqμp𝓔, Jn = nqμn𝓔):
I = A Jp + A Jn = A q ( DpLp pn0 + DnLn np0 ) (eV/VT − 1)
Put np0 = ni²/NA, pn0 = ni²/ND:
I = Is ( eV/VT − 1 )    with   Is = A q ni² ( DpLp ND + DnLn NA )

Reading the I–V curve (your three cases)

  • V = 0: ID = Is(1 − 1) = 0 A.
  • V = −1, −2, −3 V (reverse): once |V| ≫ VT, eV/VT → 0 and ID = −Is, independent of voltage. That is why Is is called the saturation current.
  • V increasing (forward): I ≈ Is eV/VT, exponential. The diode appears to "turn on" around 0.6–0.7 V in silicon because Is is so tiny (~10-15 A) that noticeable current needs V near 0.6 V.
Exam traps
  • Depletion-region diffusion current depends on the majority carriers climbing a hill; drift current on the minority carriers rolling down. Don't swap them.
  • The saturation current formula has the other side's doping crossed: the hole term uses ND (n-side donors), the electron term uses NA.
  • In the formula, use VT = 25.9 mV (or 26 mV), never 0.6 V.
  • Is doubles roughly every 5 °C in silicon (because ni² rises so fast). At a fixed current, the forward voltage falls about 2 mV per °C.

7.8 Breakdown region

Push the reverse voltage far enough and the current suddenly shoots up at the breakdown voltage VBR. It is not necessarily destructive; the junction is destroyed only if the power gets too large. Your notes list two mechanisms:

Zener mechanism

A strong electric field at the junction pulls electrons straight out of covalent bonds (quantum tunnelling). Happens in heavily doped junctions with a very thin depletion region. VBR < ≈ 5 V.

Avalanche mechanism

Carriers gain high kinetic energy from the field, collide with atoms, knock out new electron–hole pairs, which are themselves accelerated: a chain reaction. Happens in lightly doped, wide junctions. VBR > ≈ 8 V.

Between about 5 and 8 V both mechanisms contribute. Zener diodes (voltage references) use the controlled breakdown.

Explain like I'm 10

Zener: the wall is so thin and the push so strong that kids are yanked straight through the wall. Avalanche: one kid running fast crashes into two people, who then run fast and crash into four, and so on, like a snowball rolling downhill.

7.9 Your worked diode question (re-solved with checks)

A p–n diode has NA = 1018 cm-3, ND = 1016 cm-3, A = 10-4 cm², ni = 1.5×1010 cm-3, Lp = 5 μm, Ln = 10 μm, Dp = 10 cm²/s, Dn = 18 cm²/s. It is forward biased and conducts ID = 0.1 mA. Calculate (i) Is, (ii) the forward-bias voltage, (iii) the hole-injection and electron-injection components of I.

(i) Saturation current. Convert lengths: Lp = 5×10-4 cm, Ln = 10×10-4 cm. ni² = 2.25×1020.

Hole term: Dp/(LpND) = 10 / (5×10-4 × 1016) = 10/5×1012 = 2×10-12
Electron term: Dn/(LnNA) = 18 / (10-3 × 1018) = 1.8×10-14
A q ni² = 10-4 × 1.6×10-19 × 2.25×1020 = 3.6×10-3
Is = 3.6×10-3 × (2×10-12 + 1.8×10-14) = 7.26×10-15 A

(ii) Voltage. I = Is(eV/VT − 1) ⇒ 0.1×10-3 = 7.26×10-15(eV/VT − 1) ⇒ eV/VT = 1.38×1010 ⇒ V = VT ln(1.38×1010) = 0.026 × 23.35 = 0.607 V (your notes: 0.605 V).

(iii) Split the current. Divide the two components:

Ip/In = (2×10-12)/(1.8×10-14) = 111 = DpDn · LnLp · NAND
Ip + In = 0.1 mA ⇒ In = 0.1/112 = 0.0009 mA, Ip = 0.0991 mA

Meaning: 99.1 % of the current is hole injection from the heavily doped p-side into the lightly doped n-side. Making one side much heavier makes the diode "one-carrier", which is exactly the trick used for the BJT emitter (Chapter 8). (Your notes wrote Is = 7.26×10-15 A but then typed 10-13 in the next line; the 10-15 value is the one consistent with V = 0.605 V.)

Your assignment: for Si and Ge p–n diodes, which needs the higher voltage to carry a fixed forward current of 20 mA? (Hint: ni ∝ e−Eg/2kBT.)
  1. Eg(Si) = 1.1 eV > Eg(Ge) = 0.7 eV.
  2. A bigger gap ⇒ much smaller ni: ni,Si < ni,Ge.
  3. Is ∝ ni² ⇒ Is,Si ≪ Is,Ge.
  4. For the same I = IseV/VT: V = VT ln(I/Is), so the smaller Is needs the larger V.

Answer: silicon needs the higher voltage. Size of the effect: Is ratio ≈ e−(1.1−0.7)/kBT ≈ 2×10-7 (ignoring the T3 factor and mobility differences), so the voltage difference is VT ln(5×106) ≈ 0.4 V. That matches the well-known turn-on voltages of ≈0.7 V for Si and ≈0.3 V for Ge.

Extra: a Si diode has Is = 10-14 A at 300 K. Find the current at V = 0.65 V, and the voltage change that doubles the current.

I = 10-14 (e0.65/0.0259 − 1) = 10-14 × e25.1 = 10-14 × 7.9×1010 = 0.79 mA. To double it: ΔV = VT ln 2 = 0.0259 × 0.693 = 17.9 mV. (And ×10 needs 59.6 mV: the "60 mV per decade" rule.)

CHAPTER 8The Transistor and the BJT

A transistor is a valve for electricity: a small control signal governs a big flow.

Your notes p.30 to p.36

8.1 What are transistors used for, and what kinds exist?

Applications (your list): 1. switch, 2. logic gates, 3. memory devices, 4. amplifiers. Two big families:

1. Field-effect transistor (FET)

An electric field applied at the control terminal C controls the current between two terminals A and B. Almost no current enters the control terminal.

Examples: MOSFET, MESFET, MISFET (Chapters 9 and 10).

2. Junction transistor

A small amount of current injected at the control terminal C controls the (much larger) current between A and B.

Examples: BJT, hetero-junction BJT (HBT).

Explain like I'm 10

A garden tap. In a BJT you push a small amount of water into the tap's handle and that lets a big river flow. In a FET you don't push any water; you just bring an invisible magnet close to the handle and it opens up. BJT: "current controls current". FET: "voltage (field) controls current".

8.2 BJT structure

BJT = Bipolar Junction Transistor. "Bipolar" because both electrons and holes take part in conduction. It is a three-layer sandwich with two p–n junctions back-to-back:

  • Emitter (E): emits (injects) carriers. Heavily doped.
  • Base (B): the very thin, lightly doped middle layer that controls the flow.
  • Collector (C): collects the carriers. Moderately doped, physically the largest.
  • Junctions: EBJ = emitter–base junction, CBJ = collector–base junction.
  • Two flavours: npn (n–p–n; electrons do the work) and pnp (p–n–p; holes do the work). Your notes draw the pnp first and then analyse the npn, the more common type.

8.3 Band diagram of an npn transistor

Read it exactly as you read the diode: EF is flat (equilibrium, no current), the bands bend at each junction (depletion regions), and the p-type base has its bands raised relative to the n-type emitter and collector. Electrons in the emitter must climb the EBJ barrier to get into the base, and electrons in the base slide down the CBJ slope into the collector.

8.4 Modes of operation

EBJCBJModeUse
Forward biased (F.B.)Reverse biased (R.B.)Activeamplifier
Forward biasedForward biasedSaturationswitch ON
Reverse biasedReverse biasedCut-offswitch OFF
Beyond your notes: the fourth (rarely used) mode

EBJ reverse and CBJ forward is called the reverse-active mode. The BJT works but with poor gain because the collector is not designed to inject efficiently.

Active = F-R, Saturation = F-F, Cut-off = R-R.

8.5 Configurations

A BJT has three terminals but an amplifier needs an input pair and an output pair, so one terminal is shared (the "common" one):

ConfigurationCommon terminalInput portOutput port
CE (Common Emitter)Emitter (grounded)B–EC–E
CB (Common Base)Base (grounded)E–BC–B
CC (Common Collector, emitter follower)Collector (grounded)B–CE–C

Input and output characteristics

  • Input characteristic: input current vs input voltage, with the output voltage held constant.
  • Output characteristic: output current vs output voltage, with the input current held constant.
Config.Input char.Held constantOutput char.Held constant
CEIB vs VBEVCEIC vs VCEIB
CBIE vs VEBVCBIC vs VCBIE
CCIB vs VBCVECIE vs VECIB
Explain like I'm 10

Think of an electric guitar plugged into an amp. Two wires go in and two come out, but there are only three "contacts" on the gadget, so one contact is shared between "in" and "out". Which contact is shared gives you the name: common emitter, common base or common collector. CE is the champion for amplification because it boosts both current and voltage.

8.6 What happens inside an npn in active mode

Voltages: VBE forward-biases the EBJ, VCB reverse-biases the CBJ. Follow the carriers (your circled numbers ①–⑤):

  1. Emitter → base. The EBJ is forward, so electrons flow from the heavily-doped n-emitter into the p-base. This is the electron current IEn ①. Holes also flow the other way, from base into emitter: IEp ②. Total emitter current: IE = IEn + IEp. The hole part is not useful (it doesn't reach the collector).
  2. Through the base. The base is very thin, so almost all the injected electrons (now minority carriers in the base) diffuse across without recombining. A few (1–2 %) recombine with holes in the base. Those lost holes must be replaced, and that replacement is the base current IB,rec ③ that we supply.
  3. Collector sweep. The reverse-biased CBJ has a strong field that sweeps the electrons arriving at the base edge into the collector: the useful collector current ICn ④.
  4. Leakage. The reverse-biased CBJ also carries a tiny leakage current IBC,rev ⑤ (minority carriers, like the diode's Is). It is usually neglected but exists.
Your notes say

"IC will increase if we increase the electrons going from emitter to base." "IEp is not used for output current." "Due to recombination of electrons and holes in the p-region, holes are reduced, therefore we provide IB,rec (base current)."

Explain like I'm 10

Kids (electrons) run from a huge crowded playground (emitter) across a very narrow bridge (base) into a big slide (collector) that carries them away. On the narrow bridge a couple of kids trip and get stuck (recombine); the teacher (base current) must send in a few replacements. The tiny number the teacher sends controls the huge number of kids flowing. That is amplification.

Current relations
IE = IC + IB    IC ≈ ICn    IB = IB,rec + IEp (+ leakage)
Beyond your notes

IC = IS eVBE/VT (exponential, like the diode) and IB = IC/β. So VBE ≈ 0.7 V is the usual "on" voltage for silicon.

8.7 The four figures of merit

NameSymbolDefinitionWhat it saysIdeal
Base transport factorB (αT)ICn / IEnfraction of electrons injected into the base that survive the trip and reach the collector≈ 1
Emitter injection efficiencyγEIEn / (IEn + IEp)how much of the total emitter current is the useful electron current≈ 1
Current transfer ratioαICn / IEfraction of emitter current that reaches the collector (CB current gain)0.98 to 0.998
GainβIC / IBCE current gain (hFE)50 to 300
Derivations
α = ICnIE = ICnIEn × IEnIE = B × γE
IE = IC + IB ⇒ IB = IE(1 − α) ⇒ β = ICIB = α IE(1 − α) IE ⇒ β = α1 − α
and the inverse: α = ββ + 1, IE = (β + 1) IB
Explain like I'm 10

Out of 100 kids leaving the playground, γ tells you how many head the right way (the rest run backwards and are wasted), and B tells you how many of the right-way kids make it across the bridge without tripping. Multiply the two and you get α, the fraction that reaches the slide. Say α = 0.98: 98 arrive and 2 are the ones the teacher must replace, so the gain is β = 98/2 = 49.

Notice β is extremely sensitive to α: α = 0.98 ⇒ β = 49; α = 0.99 ⇒ β = 99; α = 0.995 ⇒ β = 199. Improving efficiency by half a percent doubles the gain.

8.8 How to design a good BJT: base width and doping

Your notes say
  1. Width of base should be small to reduce recombination. Wbase ↓ ⇒ recombination ↓ ⇒ collector current ↑ (and B → 1).
  2. Currents from the diode formulas: IEn = q (Dn/Ln)(ni²/NA)(eV/VT − 1) [base doping NAB] and IEp = q (Dp/Lp)(ni²/ND)(eV/VT − 1) [emitter doping NDE], with the same applied VBE. To make IEn ≫ IEp we need NDE ≫ NAB.
  3. Therefore base: lightly doped, emitter: heavily doped.
RegionDopingWidthReason
Emitterheavy (n⁺)mediuminject lots of electrons; IEp is small ⇒ γE ≈ 1
Baselight (p)very thinfew holes to recombine with ⇒ B ≈ 1; thin so electrons cross before recombining
Collectormoderatelargestcollects and dissipates power; lightly enough doped to withstand high reverse voltage
Worked: emitter NDE = 1019 cm-3, base NAB = 1017 cm-3. Assume Dp/Dn = 0.4 and equal diffusion lengths. Find γE. If B = 0.995, find α and β.
  1. IEp/IEn = (Dp/Dn)(Ln/Lp)(NAB/NDE) = 0.4 × 1 × 1017/1019 = 0.004.
  2. γE = 1/(1 + 0.004) = 0.996.
  3. α = B × γE = 0.995 × 0.996 = 0.991.
  4. β = α/(1 − α) = 0.991/0.009 ≈ 110.

If someone lowered the emitter doping to 1017 (equal to the base), the ratio would be 0.4, γE = 0.71, and β would collapse to about 2.4. That's why the emitter must be heavily doped.

Worked: a BJT has IC = 2 mA and β = 100. Find IB, IE, α. Then the same transistor is replaced by one with β = 200: what changes if IB is kept fixed?

IB = IC/β = 2 mA/100 = 20 μA. IE = IC + IB = 2.02 mA. α = IC/IE = 2/2.02 = 0.990 (also β/(β+1) = 100/101 ✔). With IB fixed at 20 μA and β = 200: IC = 200 × 20 μA = 4 mA; IE = 4.02 mA; α = 0.995. The collector current doubles because β is a property of the device: a real design problem (β varies ±50 % between parts) that engineers fix with feedback.

8.9 Metallurgical vs neutral base width

  • Metallurgical base width = the physical (initial) distance between the two metallurgical junctions.
  • Neutral base width = the part of the base that is not depleted: the region where recombination happens and carriers diffuse. It is smaller than the metallurgical width because each depletion region eats into the base.
Wneutral = Wmetallurgical − (depletion penetration into the base from EBJ) − (depletion penetration into the base from CBJ)

8.10 Base-width modulation and the Early voltage

Explain like I'm 10

Imagine the narrow bridge (the base) has walls that can slowly squeeze it. When you increase the collector voltage, the depletion region at the collector junction grows and eats into the base, so the bridge gets even shorter. A shorter bridge means fewer kids trip on it, so more of them reach the slide and the collector current creeps up. This slow rise of IC with voltage is the Early effect (base-width modulation).

  • Ideal: in the active region IC is independent of VCB (or VCE): horizontal lines, like a perfect current source.
  • Practical: the neutral base width shrinks as VCB rises ⇒ recombination ↓ and the base gradient ↑ ⇒ IC ↑. The lines have a positive slope.
  • Extrapolate those sloping lines back to IC = 0: they all meet the voltage axis at the same point −VA. VA is the Early voltage (typically 50 to 200 V).
Beyond your notes: the formula
IC = IS eVBE/VT ( 1 + VCEVA )    output resistance ro = VA + VCEIC ≈ VAIC

A larger VA means flatter lines and a better current source. Example: VA = 100 V, IC = 1 mA ⇒ ro ≈ 100 kΩ.

Exam traps for the BJT
  • Active mode means EBJ forward, CBJ reverse. Students often say "both forward".
  • The base current is not the input carriers of the collector current; it is only the small amount that replaces recombined carriers (plus the wasted hole current).
  • α is always < 1; β is always ≫ 1. β = α/(1−α), not α/(1+α).
  • Emitter arrow: it points in the direction of conventional current in the emitter: out of the emitter for npn ("Not Pointing iN"), into the emitter for pnp.

CHAPTER 9The MOS Capacitor

The heart of a MOSFET is a capacitor whose bottom plate is a semiconductor. Understand its three states and you understand how a transistor switches on.

Your second note-set, p.1 to p.3

9.1 The family tree: MOS → MOSFET → CMOS

  • MOS = Metal–Oxide–Semiconductor structure (a capacitor).
  • MOSFET = MOS Field-Effect Transistor: MOS capacitor + two n⁺ or p⁺ regions (source and drain).
  • CMOS = Complementary MOS: an nMOS and a pMOS working as a pair. The technology of essentially all modern VLSI chips.

9.2 Ordinary capacitor vs MOS capacitor

MIM (metal–insulator–metal)

Both plates are metals. C = ε₀A/d never changes, so C/A = ε/d is a constant.

MIS / MOS (metal–insulator–semiconductor)

Top plate: the gate metal. Insulator: silicon dioxide, SiO2. Bottom plate: a p-type or n-type semiconductor. C is not constant; it depends on the gate voltage VG, because the semiconductor plate can change how deep its charge sits.

Explain like I'm 10

A metal plate is like a solid wall: if you put charge on it, the charge sits right at the surface. A semiconductor plate is like a sponge: the charge can sink in at different depths depending on how hard you squeeze (the voltage). The deeper the charge sits, the farther apart the "plates" effectively are, and the smaller the capacitance.

9.3 The three states (p-type substrate)

Put a voltage VG on the metal gate, with the semiconductor body grounded. Let Qm be the charge per unit area on the metal and Qs the charge per unit area in the semiconductor (Qm + Qs = 0 always). We take a p-type substrate, as your notes do.

StateGate voltageCharge on metal QmWhat happens in the p-substrateCharge in semiconductor
Accumulation (of majority carriers)VG negative− QmNegative gate attracts holes (majority carriers). Holes pile up at the interface.+ Qs (holes)
Depletion (of majority carriers)VG small positive+ QmPositive gate pushes holes away. A region with no holes appears, exposing fixed negative acceptor ions (width w).Qs = − q NA w
Inversion (p turns to n at the surface)VG large positive (≥ Vth)+ QmThe field is now so strong that thermally generated electrons (minority carriers) are pulled to the interface and form a thin n-type layer.− [ mobile electrons + q NA wm (fixed ions) ]
Explain like I'm 10

The p-type body is a playground full of swings-with-kids (holes). Accumulation: the gate calls all kids to it; a crowd gathers at the fence. Depletion: the gate now pushes kids away; a kid-free zone appears near the fence, leaving only the chairs (fixed negative ions). Inversion: the push is so strong that the ground itself starts "making" a different type of kid (electrons) which gather at the fence. Now the surface behaves like an n-type material, even though the body is p-type. That thin layer of electrons is the channel of an nMOS transistor.

  • In depletion the charge is only the immobile ions; as VG rises the depletion width w grows.
  • Once w reaches its maximum wm, adding more gate voltage no longer widens the depletion region. Instead the extra charge shows up as mobile electrons in the inversion layer. The gate voltage at which this starts is the threshold voltage Vth.
  • For an n-type substrate everything mirrors: negative VG depletes, more negative inverts (holes form the channel), positive VG accumulates electrons.

9.4 Capacitance of the MOS structure

Two capacitors in series
Oxide capacitance (per unit area): Cox = εoxtox — independent of bias; tox = oxide thickness
Semiconductor / depletion capacitance: Cs = Cdep = εsw — depends on w, hence on VG
1C = 1Cox + 1Cs
  1. Accumulation (VG negative): holes sit right at the interface, so the semiconductor acts like a metal plate. Cdep is huge and C = Cox (C/Cox = 1).
  2. Depletion: as VG rises, w rises, Cdep = εs/w falls, so the series combination falls: C decreases.
  3. At threshold: w = wm, Cdep is at its minimum, and total C is at its minimum Cmin.
  4. Inversion: if the electron layer can follow the signal (low frequency or DC), the electrons act as the plate again and C climbs back up to Cox. At high frequency the electrons can't be generated fast enough, so C stays near Cmin. That is why your figure has several dashed curves.
Beyond your notes: real numbers for threshold
Fermi potential: φF = VT ln(NA/ni)    Max depletion width: wm = √( 4 εs φFq NA )
Vth = VFB + 2φF + √( 2 q εs NA (2φF) )Cox (VFB = flat-band voltage from work-function differences and oxide charge)

Strong inversion starts when the surface band-bending equals 2φF, i.e. the surface is as n-type as the bulk is p-type.

Worked: p-type Si, NA = 1017 cm-3, ni = 1.5×1010, oxide tox = 2 nm (εox = 3.9ε0 = 3.45×10-13 F/cm). Find Cox, wm, Cmin/Cox, and Vth ignoring VFB.
  1. Cox = 3.45×10-13 / 2×10-7 cm = 1.73×10-6 F/cm² = 1.73 μF/cm² (17.3 fF/μm²).
  2. φF = 0.0259 × ln(1017/1.5×1010) = 0.0259 × 15.71 = 0.407 V.
  3. wm = √[4 × 1.04×10-12 × 0.407 / (1.6×10-19 × 1017)] = √(1.06×10-10) = 1.03×10-5 cm = 0.103 μm.
  4. Cdep,min = εs/wm = 1.04×10-12/1.03×10-5 = 1.01×10-7 F/cm². Series: Cmin = 1/(1/1.73×10-6 + 1/1.01×10-7) = 9.55×10-8 ⇒ Cmin/Cox ≈ 0.055.
  5. Depletion charge: Qd = q NA wm = 1.6×10-19 × 1017 × 1.03×10-5 = 1.65×10-7 C/cm². Vth (ignoring VFB) = 2φF + Qd/Cox = 0.814 + 0.095 = 0.91 V.

Reading: a thinner oxide ⇒ larger Cox ⇒ smaller second term in Vth and stronger control of the channel by the gate.

Exam traps
  • "Accumulation, depletion, inversion" order depends on the substrate polarity: for p-type it goes negative → positive VG. For n-type it is reversed.
  • Cox is fixed by tox; Cdep is the one that moves. In depletion they are in series, so the total is always smaller than Cox.
  • Larger oxide thickness ⇒ weaker vertical field E = V/tox ⇒ the gate has less control.

CHAPTER 10The MOSFET

A voltage-controlled switch that draws almost no current at its gate, is very fast, and burns very little power. Billions of them make a CPU.

Your second note-set, p.4 to p.8 Sections 10.7 to 10.10 go beyond your notes

10.1 What a MOSFET is

  • MOSFET = Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor.
  • It can be used as a switch. Switching can be done at (i) very high speed and (ii) low power dissipation.
  • Four terminals: Source (S), Drain (D), Gate (G), Substrate / Bulk (B).
  • It is a unipolar device: nMOS current is due to electrons only; pMOS current is due to holes only.
Explain like I'm 10

A drawbridge. Source and drain are two banks of a river. When the gate voltage is low the bridge is up: no one crosses. When you raise the gate voltage the bridge comes down: cars (electrons) flow across. And the person cranking the bridge (the gate) never has to carry a car themselves, because they only use an electric field. That's why the gate takes almost no current.

Three things every engineer asks about a switch (your notes' list):

  1. At what VG does it turn ON? The threshold voltage Vth.
  2. RON: the ON resistance. Lower is better.
  3. Speed: the delay is τ = R C (resistance times the capacitance it must charge). Lower RON and smaller load C ⇒ faster.

10.2 Physical structure

  • nMOS: built on a p-type substrate. Two heavily doped n⁺ regions form the source and the drain. Between them, a thin SiO2 layer and the gate on top. A p⁺ contact (B) ties the body to a voltage.
  • pMOS: mirror image: an n-type substrate (or well), two p⁺ source/drain regions, an n⁺ body contact.
  • L = channel length (source to drain), W = channel width (into the page). The aspect ratio W/L is the main design knob.
  • Circuit symbols: nMOS has an arrow into the channel, pMOS has an arrow out (or a bubble on the gate in digital diagrams).

n-well CMOS process

A single wafer can't be both p-type and n-type, so a lightly doped n-well is created inside the p-substrate. The nMOS is built directly in the p-substrate and the pMOS is built inside the n-well. That is the n-well process your notes name.

10.3 Types of MOSFET

(i) By charge carrier

nMOS (electrons) and pMOS (holes).

(ii) By electrical mode

Enhancement mode: normally OFF. No channel exists between source and drain at VGS = 0; you must create one. This is the type used in CMOS.

Depletion mode: normally ON. A channel already exists at VGS = 0; you apply voltage to remove it.

Combining both classifications gives four devices: nMOS enhancement, nMOS depletion, pMOS enhancement, pMOS depletion. (Your notes list four lines; the lines "pMOS enh, pMOS dep, nMOS enh" are followed by a last line that should read "nMOS dep".)

nMOS enhancementpMOS enhancement
Carrierselectronsholes
Substratep-typen-type
Vthpositivenegative
ON whenVGS ≥ Vth (gate high)VGS ≤ Vth (gate low)
Relative speedfaster (μn > μp)slower

10.4 Biasing

nMOSpMOS
Sourcetied to the lowest potential: groundtied to the highest potential (VDD)
VGS, VDSboth positiveboth negative
Substrate (body)ground, or a negative potentialthe highest potential (VDD)
Why the body is tied that way

The source–body and drain–body p–n junctions must never be forward biased, otherwise current leaks into the substrate. So the p-substrate of an nMOS goes to the lowest voltage in the circuit, and the n-well of a pMOS goes to the highest. (Your note for pMOS shows source at "GND" in one place; in a CMOS circuit the pMOS source is tied to VDD, which is the reference that makes VGS and VDS negative relative to it. What matters is: VGS and VDS are negative.)

10.5 Operation of an nMOS

  1. Cut-off (OFF). VG = 0 V or VGS negative. There is no channel/path from source to drain for electrons. The source and drain are two n⁺ islands separated by p-type silicon (two back-to-back diodes), so no current can flow.
  2. Channel formation. Make VGS positive. As in the MOS capacitor (Chapter 9), the surface first depletes, and when VGS = VTH it inverts: a thin layer of electrons appears under the gate, joining source to drain. This is the onset of inversion. The channel is a resistor that the gate voltage controls.
  3. Vertical field: the gate field across the oxide is 𝓔 = V/tox. A thicker oxide lowers the field for the same V. The oxide capacitance Cox is fixed by tox, while Cdep depends on the state of the depletion region.
Quick check from your notes: "At what value of VG does the device turn ON?"

When the gate-to-source voltage reaches the threshold voltage: VGS ≥ VTH (for an nMOS enhancement device). Below it: cut-off. Typical VTH ≈ 0.3 to 0.7 V in modern CMOS.

10.6 The drain current: your derivation, step by step

Idea: current = charge per unit length × velocity

I = Q · v    Q = charge per unit length along the channel, v = velocity of carriers
Explain like I'm 10

Cars passing a checkpoint per second = (cars on each metre of road) × (how fast they're driving). Charge per length is the "cars per metre"; velocity is the driving speed.

  1. Inversion charge. The gate sets up a capacitor with capacitance Cox per unit area. The gate only pulls electrons into the channel once VGS exceeds Vth. The voltage that does the work is the overdrive voltage (VGS − VTH): the "extra voltage beyond VTH". With Q = C V, charge per unit length with channel width W:
    Q′ = W Cox (VGS − VTH)
  2. Effect of drain voltage. With the drain at VDS, the channel potential V(x) rises from 0 at the source (x = 0) to VDS at the drain (x = L). At position x the gate-to-channel voltage is reduced, so the total voltage experienced by the carriers is (VGS − Vth − V(x)):
    Q(x) = W Cox ( VGS − Vth − V(x) )
    Your notes tabulate it as VGS − Vth − 0, − 0.1, − 0.2, … − 1: the charge thins out towards the drain.
  3. Velocity. Drift: vd = μ𝓔 = − μ dV(x)/dx (the field is the slope of the potential).
  4. Current. Multiply charge × velocity (the sign is absorbed into the direction of I):
    I = W Cox ( VGS − Vth − V(x) ) · μ dV(x)dx
  5. Integrate along the channel. The same current I flows at every x (steady state), so we can separate variables:
    ∫x=0L I dx = μ W Cox ∫V(x)=0VDS ( VGS − Vth − V(x) ) dV(x)
    Limits: at x = 0 the source is grounded, V(x) = 0; at x = L, V = VDS.
    I L = μ W Cox [ (VGS − Vth) VDS − VDS²/2 ]
  6. Result:
    Drain current, triode (linear) region
    ID = μn Cox ( WL ) [ ( VGS − Vth ) VDS − VDS²2 ]
Careful

Your first boxed version of the result lacks the W/L factor; the final one includes it. Always include W/L. Units check: μ Cox has A/V², times V² gives A. ✔

Small VDS: the MOSFET as a resistor

For VDS ≪ VGS − Vth the VDS² term vanishes and ID ≈ μnCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth) VDS — linear in VDS. So the transistor behaves like a resistor whose value the gate controls:

RON = VDSID ≈ 1μn Cox (W/L)(VGS − Vth)

Wider transistor (W ↑), shorter channel (L ↓), higher mobility or bigger overdrive ⇒ smaller RON ⇒ faster (τ = RC).

10.7 What happens when VDS gets larger: pinch-off

Definition from your page 7
Your notes say

Pinch-off: thinning of the inversion charge due to V(x), and encroachment of the depletion layer.

Explain like I'm 10

Think of water flowing down a hose while someone squeezes the end. If you increase the water pressure difference between the two ends, the hose is squeezed most at the far end (where the gate has the weakest hold), until at the far end it's basically closed. But water still flows: it shoots through the last tiny gap at high speed, driven by the strong field there. The far-end gap barely changes, so the flow stops increasing even if you push harder. That's saturation.

  • At the drain end the gate-to-channel voltage is VGS − VDS. The channel vanishes there when this equals Vth, i.e. when VDS = VGS − Vth = Vov.
  • For VDS larger than that, the pinch-off point moves toward the source. The voltage across the remaining channel stays fixed at Vov, so the current stops growing.
Beyond your notes: the three regions
RegionCondition (nMOS)ID
Cut-offVGS < Vth≈ 0
Triode / linearVGS ≥ Vth and VDS < VGS − VthμnCox(W/L)[(VGS − Vth)VDS − VDS²/2]
SaturationVGS ≥ Vth and VDS ≥ VGS − Vth½ μnCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)²

Where the saturation formula comes from: put VDS = VGS − Vth into the triode formula: (Vov)(Vov) − Vov²/2 = Vov²/2. At this point the parabola of ID versus VDS reaches its peak (derivative zero), and beyond it the current is held flat at that peak value.

Channel-length modulation: in saturation the pinch-off point moves toward the source, so the effective length shrinks and the current rises slightly with VDS: ID = ½μnCox(W/L)Vov²(1 + λVDS). This is the MOSFET twin of the BJT Early effect (λ ≈ 1/VA).

Transconductance (gain of the transistor): gm = ∂ID/∂VGS = μnCox(W/L)Vov = 2ID/Vov.

Body effect: if the source is above the body potential by VSB, the threshold rises: Vth = Vth0 + γ(√(2φF + VSB) − √(2φF)).

Worked (beyond notes but classic): nMOS with μnCox = 100 μA/V², W/L = 10, Vth = 0.7 V. Find ID for (a) VGS = 1.7 V, VDS = 0.2 V; (b) VGS = 1.7 V, VDS = 2 V; (c) VGS = 0.5 V. Also the RON for small VDS.
  1. Vov = 1.7 − 0.7 = 1.0 V. k′(W/L) = 100 μA/V² × 10 = 1 mA/V².
  2. (a) VDS = 0.2 < Vov: triode. ID = 1 mA/V² × [1.0 × 0.2 − 0.2²/2] = 1 × (0.2 − 0.02) = 0.18 mA.
  3. (b) VDS = 2 ≥ Vov: saturation. ID = ½ × 1 mA/V² × 1.0² = 0.5 mA (independent of VDS).
  4. (c) VGS = 0.5 < Vth: cut-off, ID ≈ 0.
  5. RON ≈ 1/(1 mA/V² × 1.0 V) = 1 kΩ. With a 10 fF load, τ = RC = 1 kΩ × 10 fF = 10 ps.
Extra (delay): a nMOS switch with RON = 2 kΩ must charge a load of 50 fF. How long until it reaches 63 % of its final value? How does doubling W change it?

τ = R C = 2 kΩ × 50 fF = 100 ps (the 63 % time constant of an RC charge). Doubling W halves RON (R ∝ L/W), so τ = 50 ps if the load doesn't change. In real circuits wider transistors also add capacitance to their own drain and to the previous stage, so the gain is less than 2×.

10.8 Bringing it together: CMOS and the inverter

Explain like I'm 10

Two doors on a room, wired so exactly one is open at any time: one door leads to the "1" (power) hallway, the other to the "0" (ground) hallway. When the input is high (1), the bottom door opens and the output is connected to 0. When the input is low (0), the top door opens and the output is connected to 1. Since one door is always shut, there is never a straight path from power to ground, so almost no current is wasted while the input isn't changing. That's why CMOS uses so little power.

  • Vin = 0: nMOS off (VGS = 0 < Vth), pMOS on ⇒ Vout = VDD (logic 1).
  • Vin = VDD: nMOS on, pMOS off ⇒ Vout = 0 (logic 0).
  • Static power ≈ 0 (only tiny leakage). Dynamic power ≈ C VDD² f, only when switching.
  • Since μp ≈ μn/2 to /3, the pMOS is made 2 to 3 times wider to balance rise and fall times.

10.9 Why this course is called VLSI

One inverter needs 2 transistors, a NAND gate 4, a flip-flop about 20 to 30, a 64-bit adder thousands. Reaching millions to billions of transistors is only possible because the MOSFET is (i) tiny, (ii) needs no DC gate current, (iii) dissipates almost no static power in CMOS, (iv) can be built by the same lithography process on the same wafer. Scaling W, L and tox down together (Moore's law) is how speed rose and cost per transistor fell for 50 years.

10.10 Short-channel effects (for awareness)

  • Velocity saturation (your Chapter 6): at high lateral field carriers reach vsat, so ID ∝ Vov (linear) instead of Vov².
